translations.text: A eulogy delivered by Saint Apa Acacius, bishop of Caesarea, in the martyr shrine
built in the name of Saint Mercurius, on the day of his holy commemoration, the twentieth day of the month of Hathor.
In it he praised the many mighty deeds and wonders performed through the holy martyr Saint Mercurius. In the peace of God.
May his holy blessings be with all of us together. Amen.
Truly, light has dawned for the righteous, for this Saint Mercurius, as [?]
the sacred psalmist said, who is also the father of Christ according to the flesh, the righteous king and singer of hymns, David.
He cries out, he cries out in his sweet voice, singing with his lyre and the plectrum in his hand, saying, “Light has dawned for the righteous.”
And again, “Light has dawned in the darkness for those who are upright in heart.”
Christ himself said in the Gospel, “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father.”
Saint Mercurius [?] you see [?] boundless [?], for you were a pagan before you knew Christ well.
And when he had armed himself, he went out to war against the barbarians.
He was before [?], the lawless king, as commander of the army.
He held the arrows and the bow with which he would slaughter the barbarians.
The angel of the Lord came down from heaven and handed him the sword,
saying, “Destroy the barbarians.” [?] “We ought to show great goodwill toward them and give them honor
and glory as they deserve, with libations and sacrifices, in return for the good things they have already done for us.
We order the doors of all the temples to be opened in every city and village, from the Roman territories southward to Philae
and the Ethiopians, so that incense may be offered to the honored gods and their worship performed with great zeal.
No Christian is to appear anywhere, and the provincial governors are to pursue these Christians everywhere,
whether bishops, priests, readers, monks, laypeople, men, women, soldiers,
civilians, or officials—in short, every kind of person under the authority of my empire—to make them sacrifice to the honored gods.”
And whoever opposes my command is to be handed over to great and varied tortures until they die.”
Then Decius, the lawless emperor, ordered the herald to proclaim throughout the whole city, “Greetings to all you people!
Whether soldiers or civilians, people of every kind and every age, come, all of you, [?] the temple of the gods,
and offer sacrifices to them.” They set fire to the wood at the entrance of the temple and offered sacrifices to them, along with incense,
calves, sheep, and birds. The sky was filled with the smoke and stench of their sacrifices.
There was great turmoil among the Christians, as they were pursued and beaten.
They were dragged to the gatehouses and places of judgment and forced to sacrifice.
There were great disturbances everywhere, for the tyrant had ordered every kind of terrifying instrument of torture to be set before him,
so that the Christians would see them and be afraid: sharpened swords, iron beds,
racks on which sinews are stretched, pincers for pulling out tongues, cleavers, sharpened spikes, and cauldrons full of boiling pitch,
as well as cauldrons full of fat, iron wheels, and the rest of the terrifying instruments of torture.
For that impious emperor said, “Whoever opposes my command
I will gouge out his eyes, cut out his tongue, pull out his entrails, and cut off his toes.
And I will take out his brain. As for the rest of his body, I will throw it into the fire so that it consumes it.
When the devout people saw these things, great faintheartedness overtook them. They became afraid and gave up.
Each person was handing over his neighbor to death, and fathers were handing over their children to death.
They had forgotten the truth of nature. Brothers were dragging one another away, mistreating one another, and handing one another over, and there was great turmoil.
for everyone who confessed the name—the name of Jesus.
There was a brave young man in the army whose name was Mercurius. He was enrolled in the Martysios regiment and feared God.
He was very handsome in appearance, and the whole army loved him because of his skill.
[?] He was a native of the region of Cappadocia. He had been a Christian since childhood, along with his parents.
He was brave in battle, and God was with him in everything he did.
When the tribune saw that he was advancing in his rank and in military proficiency, he made him primicerius over his regiment.
When the king saw the young man’s bravery, he loved him and kept him close to himself, consulting him about the affairs of the palace.
After these things, while the persecution was spreading, a barbarian nation rose up against the Romans.
Emperor Decius and the entire senate were at a loss because of the great crisis and helplessness that had arisen suddenly.
The barbarians fought against them in order to take Greater Armenia from them, which lay within their borders, between them and the Romans.
Emperor Decius ordered the military units and all the Roman regiments to assemble, so that they could go out to war and fight the barbarians.
Then the king organized the divisions and regiments and marched out to war against the barbarians.
He crossed the Euphrates, the great river that lies within the borders of Armenia. He established the [?] opposite the barbarians and remained facing them with his army.
It was at that time that the courage was revealed
of this noble man, Saint Mercurius, the truly faithful one, the chief officer of the regiment of martyrs.
For he was a man whose devotion to God was complete, and he lived with every kind of godliness.
The word of God was always sweeter in his mouth than honey.
One night, while he was sleeping among the troops, after he had finished praying, he dozed off for a little while.
And look, an angel of the Lord stood over him, touched his side, and woke him. There was a sword in the angel’s right hand.
His appearance was terrifying, and he was wearing a wondrous robe. When Saint Mercurius saw him, he was very afraid.
The angel addressed him, saying, “Mercurius!” He replied, “Here I am, my lord.”
Mercurius opened his eyes, and when he saw the angel, he was afraid, thinking that he was one of the emperor’s officials or a military commander.
But the angel stretched out toward him the sword he held, drawn in his hand, and said to him:
“Take this drawn sword that is in my hand, for with it you will strike down the entire force of the barbarians.
For I am the commander-in-chief of the Lord’s army.
I have come to help you and your fellow soldiers who believe in the Lord Jesus Christ.
Now, then, prevail and be strong, for I am with you until your struggle is completed in peace.
Look, [?] the time has come, and the contest lies before you.
Fight so that you may receive your strength. An athlete does not receive a crown unless he competes properly, and the farmer who works hard is the first to receive a share of the crops.
Now, then, listen to the words I am saying to you, and do not delay in turning to the Lord your God. For a great struggle awaits you, and you will become a courageous martyr.”
For your martyrdom will become famous throughout the whole world, and everyone who hears of it will marvel at your courage.
And they will glorify God because of the mighty deeds, wonders, and acts of courage that the Lord your God has performed for you.
Great tortures will be inflicted on you by the lawless emperor, along with great suffering. But persevere, and you will receive the imperishable crown.
And everyone who is worthy to touch your body—we will save him.
Even if they are in any distress, whether in a court, in a deserted place, or in danger at sea,
or on the river, or in the misery of prison, whoever remembers your name with faith and calls upon you will be saved.
Whoever builds a shrine in your name and gives an offering in your name on the day of your commemoration,
I will place my blessing and lasting prosperity upon their dwelling, and I will never let them lack anything.
Whoever writes the book of your martyrdom, I will tear up the written record of his sins.
And I will never remember any of the things he has done, and I will grant him to you as a son in my kingdom.”
Look, I have granted you three crowns: one for wealth, one for the sufferings you will endure for my name, and another for your virginity.
Be victorious and be strong, for I am with you.
After the archangel Michael had said these things to him, he ascended to heaven in glory.
When those around him saw the great vision that had appeared, they became like dead people.
The next day, Emperor Decius ordered his army to draw up the battalions and regiments.
Once they had equipped themselves with their full battle armor, they were to take their stand for battle against the barbarians.
Then the truly courageous Saint Mercurius charged against the multitude of barbarians. He went into their midst through the power of God, who was with him.
He raised his eyes to heaven and saw the archangel Michael in the form of an army commander.
There was a drawn sword in his right hand, and he held it out toward him, saying to him, “Take courage,
and grasp this sword. Advance against the barbarians and slaughter them in the name of Christ, who gives you strength.”
Saint Mercurius stretched out his hand and took the sword from the angel Michael. He charged against the multitudes of barbarians.
He slaughtered them mercilessly in the name of Christ, until his hand stuck to the sword
because of the great quantity of blood, as he struck down the barbarians amid a very great [?], fierce on that day.
The rest fled and disappeared, as though a fire from heaven had consumed them.
When the emperor saw the act of courage that Saint Mercurius had performed through the power of God,
who was with him. He rejoiced greatly over the victory and this triumph that had come to the Romans.
The emperor bestowed great honors and abundant riches on Saint Mercurius. He [?] and made him commander of the Martusion regiment.
After these things, Emperor Decius gave orders to all the troops, the military units, the regiments, and the commanders,
and the generals, the patricians, and the entire Roman senate, that they should all assemble at the temple of Apollo and offer sacrifices.
Then, when the blessed Mercurius saw the great delusion that had seized the emperor and the army through the devil,
he withdrew from them and went into his house. He pleaded with the Lord, saying, “Lord Almighty, Father of our Lord Jesus Christ,
have mercy on your creature, whom you yourself made, and sweep away the stumbling block that the devil has cast into the heart of all humanity.
And give steadfastness to the heart of the people and of everyone who fears your holy name.
Lord, give strength to your churches, so that everyone may believe in your holy name.
Glory to you and your good Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.”
When the emperor came to the entrance of the temple, his entire army gathered so that they might all offer sacrifices, each one according to his rank.
The turn of Saint Mercurius also came for him to offer sacrifice, but they did not find him among the army.
When the emperor looked for him, he found him sitting in his house in sackcloth and ashes,
grieving deeply over the great division that had come upon the whole inhabited world through the devil.
Then some men from his regiment approached the emperor and slandered the blessed Mercurius, saying, “Our lord the emperor,
live forever! Your honored authority has ordered people of every nation to sacrifice to the honored gods.
Now look: those close to you and those attached to you are despising your honored decree. Mercurius, then,
who holds authority in your kingdom—you exalted him and granted him the rank of count over the regiment—
And since the entire Roman army obeyed him, honored him, and submitted to him because of the great honor you bestowed on him,
look, he despises your authority! He did not assemble with us at the temple to offer sacrifices to the gods.
Instead, he went to his house and deprived himself of his rank. He has brought shame on the glory of the Romans and defiled the sacred laws.
We found him inside his house, sitting in sackcloth and ashes, praying with tears to the Lord his God.
He is also persuading everyone to turn away from worshiping the gods. He has made them follow Jesus the Nazarene, who was crucified,
saying, ‘This is God, who made heaven and earth.’ In this way he has made everyone withdraw from the gods.”
The emperor said to those reporting these things, “Are these things you are telling me true,
about Mercurius, who is attached to me—that he despises my gods? Nevertheless, let two officials who are here
go and summon him, so that I may learn whether these things you are telling me about him are true or not.”
Then they brought the blessed Mercurius before the emperor Decius.
His eyes were full of tears, and he wore a humble garment. They made him stand before the emperor.
When he saw him in his humble appearance, he shook his head, puzzled over what had happened.
Then he spoke to him, saying, “Mercurius, tell me what has happened to you, and why you have despised this great honor and the rank
that I gave you. I made you worthy of the gods’ care, yet you have considered the rank I gave you above all the rest of the army to be nothing.
“Now, then, tell me through whom this delusion came upon you.”
The Roman army gathered at the temple to offer sacrifices to the gods, as is right. But you alone separated yourself from the regiment.
In any case, tell me who you are, what country you come from, and whether your parents called you by this name.”
The blessed Mercurius answered and said to the emperor, “Do you want to know who I am and to
which religion I belong? Listen to my origins. In this world, I am from Cappadocia.
But in truth I am from the heavenly Jerusalem, the capital city of the saints. The name my parents first gave me was
Philopator, which means ‘one who loves his father.’ But when I became a soldier, I was named Mercurius by the chief officer of the regiment.
I am the servant of Jesus Christ, my Lord, the Son of the living God.
When the emperor heard these things, he cried out in great anger.
He shook his head, saying, ‘Mercurius, give up this defiance and this madness. Go into the temple and sacrifice to the great god Apollo.’
‘Then go to your regiment, to your fellow soldiers, and receive your rank as before.’
Saint Mercurius said before the lawless emperor: Let this be clear to you, lawless emperor:
I will not sacrifice to your Apollo, a worthless image, and abandon my God, who created heaven and earth and everything.
‘For I am a Christian.’
‘Openly, I will renounce military service in this world. I have no need of your rank. I am the servant of Christ Jesus, the Son of the living God.’
Emperor Decius answered him: Mercurius, until now I have not believed the things
your accusers told me about you. For I know that they accused you out of envy,
when they saw the great honor I gave you among the entire regiment and the army.
‘Now, then, obey me and sacrifice to the gods.’
‘Do not let this matter force me to forget the affection I had for you, strip you of your rank, and inflict severe punishments on you.’
The blessed man answered the emperor, saying, ‘Friendship with this world is nothing; it is hostility toward God.’
‘And honors of this kind are temporary.’
But God's glory endures forever. So now, do not trouble yourself in vain.
For I am a Christian. I will not sacrifice to your abominable gods. So do whatever you wish to me.
Decius said to him: Mercurius, offer sacrifice! Do not die a terrible death! Blessed Mercurius said to him:
Let one word be enough for you, emperor. I will certainly not obey you and serve foreign gods and abandon my God, Jesus Christ.
When Decius heard this, he became extremely angry. He ordered that Mercurius be stripped of his clothes and stretched out
by ten soldiers, and that they beat him with raw oxhide whips until the ground beneath him grew hot with his blood.
The emperor Decius said to him, ‘Mercurius, you have tasted the beginning of the tortures, how terrible they are. Will you sacrifice or not?’
The blessed Mercurius answered, “As long as I have my Lord Jesus Christ helping him, I am not troubled by your tortures.”
‘For I am the servant of my Lord Jesus Christ, who helps me. He is the king of those in heaven and those on earth.’
When the emperor Decius heard these things, he said, ‘Mercurius, obey me and sacrifice to the gods. Escape severe tortures, so that you do not die miserably.’
‘Until now I have spared you and been patient with you.’
‘For I do not want to harm you, especially since you became my companion by fighting for me in the war.’
‘Obey me and sacrifice to the gods.’
‘Do not destroy your youth through cruel tortures.’
‘I have compassion for your youth and for your friendship.’
Blessed Mercurius answered: Every suffering I undergo because of my confession of God
is worth more to me than a holy reward. For the sufferings of the present time are not worthy of the glory that will be revealed to us.
When Emperor Decius heard these things, he said: If you have set your heart on foolish words,
and have counted the honors of the Romans as nothing, and have refused to sacrifice to righteous gods
according to the decrees of the senate, and have not obeyed the laws of the emperors, I, in turn, will punish you
as your foolishness deserves, and I will see whether the God in whom you have trusted can rescue you from my hands.
Saint Mercurius answered the emperor, saying, “It is written in the holy Apostle: ‘Who can separate us from the love of God?
Is it trouble, or distress, or persecution, or hunger, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword? As it is written: For your sake we are being killed all day long.’
For we are convinced that neither death nor life, neither angels nor rulers nor authorities,
neither present things nor things to come, will be able to separate us from the love of Christ.
When the blessed Mercurius said these things, Emperor Decius became angry. He ordered them to put him on the rack and scrape him.
The executioners scraped him until the bone of his spine was exposed.
But the blessed man did not stop praising God, saying: Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of the Father,
born of the holy Virgin Mary, who took flesh from the true ewe to redeem the whole race of Adam
and free us from slavery to sin, I thank you because you have made us worthy of your abundant goodness.
Listen to me today.
I am your servant Mercurius.
Make me worthy of your holy calling, a sharer in your holy sufferings, and a faithful witness to your divinity.
Now then, my Lord, do not abandon me, and do not turn away from me, for troubles are pressing upon me and snares have fallen upon me.
But give me strength, my Lord, so that I may finish my struggle in peace. Do not let my enemies rejoice over me, and do not let them say among the nations, ‘Where is their God?’”
While he was saying these things, a voice came to him, saying, “Take courage, my soldier Mercurius. Endure, my chosen mighty warrior.
For I am with you, strengthening you, and I will be with you as a protector, helping you in every suffering
that you will endure in my name. Do not grow weak or be dismayed by the tortures.
I am with you, strengthening you until you finish your struggle with courage.”
Immediately the archangel Michael greeted him and marked his whole body with a seal.
Immediately the [?] split and broke in two, and the bonds with which he was bound
They untied him. He sprang up and stood, with no injury at all in him, and he was glorifying God.
When the king saw what had happened, he was filled with anger. He said, “Since this man has said, ‘We have a weak suit of armor,’
I order that he be stretched out, fastened to the nails, and pulled taut, neither in heaven nor on earth, a cubit [?].”
When they had done this to him, the emperor said, “Where now are the weapons in which you trust? By Zeus, the greatest of the great gods, they have stretched you out completely!”
The holy man looked up to heaven and said, “Lord, help me! I am your servant.” Again the king gave orders
to tear his body with sharp instruments and whips, and afterward to spread burning coals beneath him,
so that he would burn little by little. But the fire was extinguished by the righteous man's blood as it flowed down.
But the holy man recovered his strength with great fortitude during this further torture.
The emperor Decius had him taken away, lest he die too quickly, and they hurriedly threw him into a dark place.
The soldiers carried him away half dead, with only a little breath remaining in him, thinking that he had died.
A little later, at that very hour, an angel of the Lord appeared to him and said, “Peace to you, victorious warrior!”
When he had received this, the angel healed the wounds on his body and set him on his feet, healthy. Once he had risen, he stood glorifying God, who helped him.
After this, the emperor ordered them to bring him before the tribunal.
When the emperor [?] him, he said to him, “They took you away from me half dead. How is it that you are walking now? Perhaps there is not even a wound on your body!”
Then he ordered the guards who stood there to examine his body.
They said to the emperor, “By your power, O pious emperor, his entire body is healthy. There is no injury in it, as though they had never touched him at all.”
Decius himself said, “He will certainly say, ‘It is Christ who healed me.’ Did you bring a physician into the prison to treat him?”
They said, “By your honored Majesty, who rules over the whole inhabited world, no human healer has healed him.”
“But [?] we do not know how he will die while he is alive, or how to make him stop. For the magic of the Christians is a hard wood that does not rot or decay.”
Yet today he stands here healthy.
The emperor was filled with anger and said to him, “Tell me truthfully who healed you without magic.”
Saint Mercurius answered, “My Lord Jesus Christ, the physician of souls and bodies, is the one who grants me healing.
As he has said, sorcerers, magicians, and idol worshippers are strangers to him, and he will bind them
with bonds that cannot be untied and hand them over to the fire of Gehenna, because they did not acknowledge the God who created them.”
He said, “I will wear out your body with harsh tortures. Let me see whether the Christ in whom you believe will heal you.”
Saint Mercurius said, “I trust in my Lord Jesus Christ that even if you inflict many punishments on me, you will not be able to shake me.”
“For he said, ‘Do not fear those who will kill your bodies but have no power to kill your souls.’
“‘Rather, fear the one who has power to destroy both your soul and your body in Gehenna.’”
Then the king ordered them to bring a red-hot piece of iron and put it beneath his elbows,
and burning torches beneath his sides. When they did this, instead of smoke, a sweet fragrance arose and spread
to everyone in that place. Although they tortured him all the more, he neither groaned nor wept. The king said to him,
“Where is your physician now? Let him come and heal you! For you said that he can even raise the dead.”
But Saint Mercurius said to him, “Do whatever you want, for you have authority over my body.
But God is the master of my soul. Even if you destroy my body, my soul will remain imperishable.”
Again the emperor ordered them to hang him upside down and bring a large stone and fasten it to his neck, so that he would choke and die quickly.
But God's power and grace dwelt in the martyr, and he endured this torture for a long time.
When King Decius saw that the martyr endured the punishments steadfastly and that no torture overcame him,
he ordered them to remove that stone from his neck, bring a whip of rawhide with four thongs, and beat him until the ground was soaked with his blood.
But the noble man withstood this further torture, firm as a stone of adamant.
And he said, “I thank you, my Lord, because you have made me worthy to suffer for your holy name.”
When the king saw that his resolve was unchangeable and that he could not persuade him to offer sacrifice,
he took counsel, for he was in a hurry to go to Rome. He sentenced him to execution by the sword, saying,
“Mercurius has insulted the gods and despised the sacred decrees of our benevolence.
He has treated our power as nothing. I order that he be taken to the city of Cappadocia and beheaded there, with everyone watching.”
For anyone who has received honor from the emperor, if he opposes his command, will be subjected to blows, and finally he will be handed over to the sword.
Those appointed to carry him lifted him up, put him on a pack animal, and tied him onto it, because the martyr's body had fallen apart on every side. He had become like a corpse.
They traveled along the long road, and after a few days they reached the city of Caesarea. Then they lowered him down little by little.
But the Lord stood over him and said to him, “Mercurius, come and rest beside me, since you have finished your race.
You have kept the faith. Receive your crown of victory, which has been appointed for you to inherit.”
When the Lord appeared to him, the martyr gained strength. He said to those in charge of him, “Do what you have been ordered to do
quickly. May the Lord, who calls everyone to repentance, make you worthy of his grace.”
For he is rich and freely gives gifts, without begrudging them, to those who come to him.
After he said these things, they beheaded him. He completed the good confession of our Savior on the twenty-fifth of November, that is, Athor.
A great miracle occurred, worthy of being remembered. After the martyr had died, his body became white as snow,
giving off a sweet fragrance like the finest incense. Because of this sign, many people became Christians.
They laid the saint in a publicly visible shrine, where many miracles and healings take place.
Glory to God the Father and his only Son, Jesus Christ our Lord,
and to the Holy Spirit, now and always, forever and ever. Amen.
The martyrdom of Saint Mercurius, the commander and holy martyr of Christ, which he completed on this day, the twenty-fifth of the month of Athor. In peace. 99.
In the time of Decius and Valerian, when they were ruling as emperors in the great city of Rome,
they issued a decree by unanimous agreement, requiring everyone everywhere to sacrifice to the gods and pour out offerings to them.
They summoned all the senators and laid before them what they had decided upon in this unanimous agreement.
When they found that the senators were of one mind with them, they rejoiced greatly, saying, “We thank our immortal gods, who have revealed
this unanimous decision.” And at that very hour,
they ordered a decree to be issued, written as follows in an imperial letter, in this form:
Decius and Valerian, the sovereign and pious emperors, together with all the senators of Rome,
wrote to those living everywhere: “We considered it necessary to inform you of what is pleasing in our sight.
For long ago we discovered that it is the gods of our ancestors who uphold our empire
and grant good things to everyone under our authority. We know their acts of kindness toward us and their gifts,
just as they have said. Indeed, through them we have enjoyed victory over all the nations. Not only that, but they have also supplied us with abundant crops through the temperate climate.
For this reason, we and all the senators have issued this decree by unanimous agreement and with great earnestness, requiring everyone everywhere,
free people and slaves, soldiers and civilians, to bring sacrifices to the gods and pour out offerings to them, with prayers and supplications.
But if anyone sets about rejecting our sacred decree, which we have commanded by unanimous agreement,
our authority commands that such a person be shut up in a dark prison and subjected to severe torture.”
But whoever obeys our command will receive great honor from us.
“But if he disobeys us and our decree, he will be handed over to punishment by the sword, or to death by [?], or he will be given as food to the wild beasts and the birds.”
“Christians, especially, will be subject to a sentence of this kind.”
Those who obey our decree will live in happiness.
When the emperor’s command was proclaimed, the whole city of Rome was filled with turmoil and fear. Not only that, but all the other cities were also thrown into turmoil,
because this same decree had been sent to them. The governors in each city ordered the people
to carry out quickly what they had been commanded to do.
At that time, the barbarians began a war against the Romans.
As they made them change color, they also prepared their army to fight against them.
They ordered the military units in every place and every city to come and assist them.
When they came from each of the cities, eagerly prepared, the military unit of those called the Martysians also came,
who were stationed in First Armenia, under a tribune named Sardonicus.
Decius went out to war, while Valerian remained in Rome, administering the affairs of the empire.
The war intensified between the barbarians and the Romans, and they stood against one another.
After they had continued like this for many days, one of the regiment called the Martenses, whose name was Mercurius, saw a tall man of light,
wearing radiant clothes. He held a drawn sword in his right hand and said to him, “Mercurius, do not be afraid or be alarmed.”
For I have been sent to help you and to reveal you as a victor.
Take this sword from me and go out against the barbarians. When you defeat them, do not forget the Lord your God.
When this man fell into a trance, he thought that the one speaking with him was one of the emperor's high officials.
When he had taken the sword and was filled with the Holy Spirit, he went into their midst and killed their leader and many others with him,
so that his arm grew weary from striking, and because of the great amount of blood, his hand stuck to the sword’s handle.
This was how the barbarians fled and were slaughtered before the Romans.
Then, when Emperor Decius learned of this mighty man’s courage,
he summoned him and gave him a high rank. He made him general and commander over his entire army.
Decius, thinking that he had won the war through the providence of the gods, rejoiced greatly.
He distributed a great deal of money among the soldiers. That day the regiments were sent back to their own stations.
He himself held celebrations in every city through which he passed on his way to Rome.
One night, while the army was asleep, an angel stood over Mercurius in the form of the man whom he had seen during the war. He prodded his side and woke him.
When he saw him, he became afraid. But the angel said to him, “Do you remember the words I spoke to you during the war, Mercurius?
Be careful not to forget the Lord your God, for you must fight well for his name and receive your crown of victory in the kingdom of heaven,
which he has prepared for all who love him.” When he had said this, he immediately withdrew from him.
When the blessed man came to his senses, he remembered the words and marveled at the power of God’s love for humanity.
For he had heard about the Christian faith through his parents.
His father was Gordian, and he was the chief officer of this same regiment. The young man was approaching twenty-five years of age.
For he had often heard his father say, “Blessed is the one who serves as a soldier under the King of heaven.
He will grant him great, imperishable honors, and he will fight on his behalf against his enemies.
For that King is the one who created everything by his word.
He established heaven like a vault and adorned it with shining stars, and the earth with beautiful flowers,
which give off a sweet fragrance to provide people with refreshment and healing. He also made the sea for ships to sail upon and made it a place where fish are nourished.
And he is the one who is coming to judge the living and the dead and to repay each
person according to his deeds.” When Saint Mercurius recalled in his heart his father’s words and the revelation he had seen,
he became deeply distressed and began to weep and sigh, saying, “Woe to me, a sinner!
I am like a fruitless branch that has sprouted without having within it the root of the knowledge of God’s glory.”
While he was still speaking, the emperor immediately sent two of those called silentiaries,
with some others accompanying them, to summon him to his presence, because he was his adviser.
He asked to be excused from going, saying, “My body is weak.” The emperor said nothing that day. But the next day Decius again sent for him in the same way.
When he came to him, they consulted with one another about the matter at hand.
The emperor said to him, “Let us go, Mercurius, to the great temple of Artemis and offer sacrifices to her.”
When the emperor set out, a large crowd followed him.
But the blessed Mercurius turned back and hid in the praetorium.

The Sixth Miracle of Saint Mercurius
Now, when they began building the shrine of Saint Mercurius, they did so with great diligence, for there were abundant materials and many people working on the holy man's sanctuary.
After this, a man from the city came passing by. He saw the timber at the martyr’s shrine and was amazed. He wanted a piece of wood that was lying there.
He said, “I need this piece of wood, and I will take it.”
He went over to the wood, loaded it onto himself, and walked with it until he had gone a short distance into the city.
Then he wandered about, not knowing where he was going, because the saint had confused his mind,
until he came and stood at the door of the poor man, the steward of Saint Mercurius.
This was the man to whom the saint used to appear. The other man did not know where he was going.
The saint spoke to the steward, saying to him, “What are you doing sitting here? Look, timber has been stolen from my shrine.
Get up and go to the door of your house. You will find the man with this timber loaded on him, wandering about without knowing where he is going.
For I am the one who confused him. I did not let him know where he was going until he came here, so that you could see him with the timber he stole loaded on him.”
When he saw the house, and it was opened for him, he recognized the man as the steward of the martyr’s shrine. His senses returned to him.
Immediately he cried out, “The God of Saint Mercurius is one! Have mercy on me! Do not be angry with me and bring harm upon me, for I have sinned against you and stolen your timber.”
The saint also said to his steward, “Say this to the man: ‘Why [?] come and spend a day doing harm to my shrine?
Even the timber that he gave to my shrine as a ransom for the salvation of their souls—you went and stole it.’”
But because of God’s mercy, look, I have released you. Take the wood and put it back in its place as it was, and go home.
When he gets up in the morning, let him tell everyone what happened to him, so that the others will be afraid and will not steal the timber of my sanctuary again and make me bring disaster upon them.
When he had said these things, he hid himself from him.
The poor man got up and came outside. He found the man with the wood loaded onto him, standing at the door of his house, not knowing where he was going.
He was saying, “Saint Mercurius, have compassion on me and have mercy on me, for I have sinned, my lord!”
The poor man spoke to him: “My dear brother, where are you coming from with the wood loaded on you? I tell you

The man told him how he had taken the wood and how Saint Mercurius had confused his mind until he came to the door of the poor man’s house, unaware of where he was.
The man to whom Saint Mercurius [?] passed on to the man who had taken the wood every word that Saint Mercurius had spoken to him.
When the man heard this, he was amazed and said, “Not just [?] one single day, but if the God of Saint Mercurius

Immediately he recovered his composure and went to his house, glorifying God and his holy martyr. He slept until morning.
When daylight came, he proclaimed throughout the whole city what had happened to him.
He went to the place from which the wood came, loaded it onto his neck while everyone watched him, and carried it to the saint’s sanctuary. He put it in the place from which he had taken it.
Great fear fell upon everyone who saw him, and they did not touch any other property belonging to the sanctuary again until it was completed.
And the man did not stop working, laying bricks for the saint’s sanctuary, until they had completed it.
And he was giving glory to the God of Saint Mercurius.
The Seventh Miracle of Saint Mercurius
Listen again, my beloved, to another great wonder, to the glory of God and Saint Mercurius.
Now, when they had beautifully constructed the sanctuary with every kind of craftsmanship, they fitted it with a wooden screen made of persea wood.

Then they fashioned an extremely beautiful arch of persea wood.
When the crowds gathered to raise it, a few of the workers said to one another jokingly, “If only
Saint Mercurius were willing to help us build a martyr’s shrine for him and make this arch of [?] produce ripe fruit! Even if it were unripe, we would eat it.”
But suddenly, while the words were still coming out of their mouths, the wood put out branches laden with fine, ripe persea fruit.
When the crowds saw what had happened, they cried out in a loud voice,
giving glory to God and his holy martyr, who performs these mighty deeds and these many wonders.
And some devoted people took away some of the fruit and kept it in their homes as a protection.
Oh, how many healings came about through that fruit! The crowds ate and were satisfied, and they thanked God and his holy martyr, Saint Mercurius.
Everyone in the city and its surrounding area heard about it, young and old alike, and they all came together
to see this great miracle. Men and women came to look at what had happened, which the righteous man had done.
There was also a Jew in the city called Gaipius. He was savage [?] toward everyone, but especially toward the Christians.
He too heard about the great miracle that had happened in the saint’s sanctuary and said, “I will go and see
whether these things that the Christians are saying are true or not. Perhaps they are lying.”
He ordered Entenoun, a slave of his, to saddle a white female mule for him.
He mounted it and said to his slave, “Come, let us see the ridiculous thing these Christians are doing.”
Then they traveled together until they came to the sanctuary of Saint Mercurius. The Jewish man went inside, mounted on his animal.
One of the young Christian boys working on the sanctuary said to him, “Where are you going, you godless man, bringing this animal into God’s church?”
But the Jewish man paid no attention to him at all. Instead, he went on, stopped, and looked up at the arch, laden with fruit and leaves as though it were rooted in the ground.
And the Jewish man said, “Who put these leaves from elsewhere on the crowns, lying about the saint by saying that he did this?”
The young boy of Aphthartus, who had spoken earlier about the animal he was riding, answered him, saying, “The one who will strike you shortly

And immediately, Saint Mercurius came in through the door, with an angel walking beside him and his spear in his hand.
He said to him, “What are you doing here, you worthless man? This is no place for mockery. You have let your horse come inside. These leaves

Immediately he pierced him through the middle with his lance, and his intestines came out.
No one could see the saint except the Jewish man whom the saint had struck.
But they saw the man lying stretched out, unconscious. They did not know what had happened to him.
Afterward the man cried out in a loud voice, saying, “Saint Mercurius, help me in this hour of distress!”
I will never again spend any time mocking any saint. And if you have mercy on me

When he had said these things, he was lying stretched out, half dead.
After this, the angel of the Lord spoke to Saint Mercurius: “Wave your spear over him, if he is going to believe in our true king,
Christ. A sinner is better than a righteous person who is going to sin. There is joy among the angels over a sinner

And the saint released him.
When he came to his senses, he recounted everything that had happened to him to the crowd gathered there.

After this, the man got up and went home, telling his wife and his servants
